title: LLM swap alignment and staging playbook
meeting_header: Date: 2027-08-03 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 48m | Recording: https://call.recordings/ff/nt/8421 | Redwood: Alex Morgan, Sofia Reyes | Novaterra: Jordan, Priya, Marcus
summary: Intro + parity mapping walkthrough for moving production endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together into Redwood. Covered tokenization differences, sampling semantics, embedding distance normalizations, console staging, and a proposed staging playbook (smoke tests, perf bench, rollout). Agreed next steps: share parity spreadsheet, security pack, and schedule a 1-week pilot run in dedicated capacity.
topics: parity gaps: generation semantics, embeddings, streaming
console + Optimize capabilities for staging and rollouts
transcript: [00:00] Alex (Redwood-AE): Alright, thanks for jumping on. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the account, and Sofia is our SE. Jordan, Priya, Marcus — nice to e-meet you.

[00:12] Jordan (Novaterra CTO): Hey Alex, hey Sofia — thanks. We tried to put an agenda in the calendar, mostly around mapping parity and a staging plan. We're targeting a pilot in two weeks if feasible.
[00:25] Sofia (Redwood-SE): Totally, we'll try to keep this practical. Quick question, when you say pilot, is that traffic mirrored or a cutover?
[00:32] Priya (ML Eng): We're thinking mirrored first — we want to compare outputs token-for-token and latency under typical load. Also we'll run our eval suites against samples.
[00:44] Marcus (DevOps): And we need to know networking — we run in a VPC and we have strict egress controls. Private deployment is something we'd consider if the SLA looks good.

[00:55] Alex: Great. High level: we'll walk through parity mapping (sampling, stop tokens, embeddings), then console features for staging and Optimize recommendations. We'll flag any known gotchas for OpenAI/Anthropic/Together conversions.
[01:10] Jordan: Cool. One thing — Together's temp behavior seemed different for low temps; we saw some deterministic drift. Does Redwood normalize temperature semantics across model families?

[01:22] Sofia: Good call. So Redwood doesn't rewrite model internals; we expose the model's sampling params but provide a mapping table. For Together-like models we note that 'temperature=0' can still produce variability because of tokenization and float math; our parity doc suggests using deterministic decoding (top-k/top-p settings) for strict equivalence checks.
[01:47] Priya: When you say tokenization, are you referring to BPE differences? We have embeddings and generation endpoints that depend on tokenization alignment.

[01:55] Sofia: Yes — tokenizer differences are the single biggest source of mismatches. We recommend shipping the same tokenizer artifacts or using our adapter layer that can ingest an external tokenizer. We'll share the script that checks token counts and token ids across providers.

[02:10] Jordan: Perfect. Also embeddings — we use cosine similarity and we currently normalize by L2 on our side. Do Redwood embeddings guarantee the same scale and dimensional ordering as Anthropic/OpenAI?

[02:22] Alex: Models differ; so no hard guarantee. Our parity spreadsheet includes recommended normalization (L2) and a small transformation for a few models where orientation changed. For the pilot we'll run a set of vectors and provide a delta report.
[02:36] Marcus: On the infra side, can you walk us through dedicated capacity vs hosted? What's the latency difference we should expect for a 8k-context model?

[02:46] Sofia: Hosted for the same instance types typically hits SLOs in the low 100s ms per token for streaming on 8k context with optimized kernels. Dedicated gives you pinned GPU pools and predictable tail latencies — less jitter. We'll give you benchmarks from our catalog for the model family you listed.
[03:05] Priya: Any special notes about KV cache behavior? We rely on prefix caching for multi-turn sessions.

[03:13] Sofia: Redwood supports KV cache with transparent prefix caching and you'll see the same semantics as typical llama-like runtimes. The main parity check is ensuring your cache keys (session ids) are consistent and that you don't strip system tokens.
[03:28] Alex: We're uploading a parity workbook after this — it has sections: tokenizer check, generation params, embeddings mapping, latency bench plan, and QA smoke tests for NER/fact-checking.
[03:38] Jordan: Nice. Can you show the console staging flow? We want to do a canary -> A/B -> full rollout pattern, and trace per-route token costs.

[03:47] Sofia: Yes — demo time. (screen share) On the Console you can create a rollout and attach a test suite. There's an Optimize suggestion pane that recommends batching and quantization profiles based on your workload. You can also pin model variants by route and set auto-fallback policies if a variant exceeds latency thresholds.
[04:10] Marcus: That auto-fallback is big for us — if a model spikes we need instant fallback to a cheaper model without losing availability.
[04:17] Sofia: Exactly. You can set region, cost, and latency policy priorities. We'll demo a failover later in the pilot runbook.
[04:25] [10s crosstalk] Speaker 6: mm-hmm, yeah

[04:35] Alex: Quick security checklist — we support SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations (AWS KMS & HSM). For private deployments we provide an air-gapped option and can ship an on-prem bundle if required.
[04:50] Jordan: We're SOC 2 in-flight; can we get the security pack and a sample SOC2 report?
[04:55] Alex: Yes — I'll include the security pack and our ATO docs. Also the standard SOC2 attestation is in the security bundle.
[05:05] Priya: About performance tests: we want a script that runs our 50-sample eval set across both providers concurrently and produces token-delta and embedding cosine diffs.
[05:13] Sofia: We have a benchmarking harness in the repo. We'll add your eval set and produce a CSV with per-sample metrics. It also measures tail latency and memory utilization.
[05:25] Jordan: Great. A couple of gotchas we've seen: stop-sequence handling — sometimes OpenAI stops on '###' and Anthropic treats it differently. How do you recommend normalizing stops?

[05:36] Sofia: Normalization is necessary. Our parity workbook suggests canonicalizing stop tokens in pre-processing and adding explicit end-of-sequence tokens where a provider is ambiguous. We'll add automated checks to the smoke tests.

[05:50] Alex: Let's talk rollout playbook — proposed steps: 1) mirror traffic and run token-level diffs, 2) run functional evals (QA, NER, extraction), 3) perf bench at 10/50/100 RPS, 4) canary 5% with fallback rules, 5) A/B for a week, then gradual shift. Total pilot ~1 week + 3 day canary.
[06:14] Marcus: For network policy: we need a CIDR allow list. Does Redwood provide static egress IPs for hosted?
[06:22] Alex: We can provide egress ranges; for strict whitelisting we recommend Dedicated or Private so you can keep controls internal. We'll put the IP list in the security pack.
[06:33] Priya: Regarding sampling — temperature mapping table would help. Sometimes the same nominal temperature leads to different entropy across models.
[06:40] Sofia: We'll attach a mapping table and recommend deterministic decoders for parity checks. For production you can tune temp for quality.
[06:49] Jordan: Any notes on function-calling and structured outputs? We use schema enforcement for tools and want exact JSON outputs.

[06:58] Sofia: We support function/tool calling. The main parity issue is serialization; our SDK provides a strict JSON mode that fails the call if the model returns invalid schema — we recommend enabling that for production.
[07:10] Alex: Also note streaming differences — some providers stream token-by-token; we emulate chunked streaming in the client with the same events so your frontend shouldn't need changes.
[07:20] Priya: About cost modeling: can you show how Console surfaces token-level spend?

[07:26] Sofia: In Console you get per-route cost, per-token breakdown (inferred model compute vs I/O), and cost forecasts. Optimize will also suggest batching windows and cache TTLs to reduce unit cost.
[07:40] Jordan: That suggestion engine — is it automated or do we run profiling?
[07:44] Sofia: Both. It auto-suggests from a sampling of your traffic and you can run a profiler for a deeper run that simulates higher RPS.

[07:53] [pause] Alex: Ok, let's do a quick demo of the parity workbook and the sample CSV outputs. (Sofia shares spreadsheet) — see the tokenizer sheet, generation mapping, and embedding diffs columns.
[08:05] Priya: I see a column 'token_shift' — is that when token ids mismatch?
[08:09] Sofia: Correct — small shifts show where token boundaries differ. We flag those samples for manual review.
[08:15] Jordan: Good. On access controls: can we map to our internal groups via SAML groups?
[08:22] Alex: Yes, SAML group-to-team mapping is supported. We'll include an example SAML assertion mapping in the pack.
[08:30] Marcus: For the pilot, who from Redwood will be on-call?
[08:34] Alex: I'll be the AE lead, Sofia will be SE lead during the pilot, and we'll assign an on-call infra engineer for the bench day. We'll include contact info in the kickoff email.
[08:45] Jordan: Ok, timeline — if we get deck and security pack today, we can sign off on pilot scope tomorrow and start mirrored traffic the following Monday.
[08:54] Alex: Sounds reasonable. We'll send the parity workbook, security pack, and a dedicated runbook with the bench script.
[09:00] [background noise, brief interruption] Speaker 6: ...sorry, laptop notifications

[09:12] Sofia: A few more technical notes: 1) quantization profiles — for certain models, 4-bit quantization changes small decimals, so we recommend validating QA for any low-bit profile. 2) batching windows — we have continuous batching, but you can set max-latency if you need hard SLOs.
[09:36] Priya: Okay, for our smoke tests, do you recommend a deterministic seed for cross-provider equality checks?

[09:42] Sofia: Use deterministic decoding plus fixed seeds where supported, otherwise rely on structural checks (like parse tree equality) for function outputs. We'll include examples in the workbook.
[09:55] Jordan: Any prior customers migrated from Together? We had a weird subtle drift with Together that wasn't reproducible elsewhere.

[10:03] Alex: We have a couple of customers in analytics who've moved from Together; the common theme was tokenizer and sampler mapping. We'll anonymize notes from those projects and include a short lessons-learned doc.
[10:16] Marcus: What's the expected effort from our side? How many engineer-days?

[10:21] Alex: For the initial pilot: ~2-3 engineer-days to wire the harness and run benches, plus one SE day from our side for setup and validation. If you opt for dedicated, there's some provisioning lead time.
[10:34] Priya: For provisioning, we might prefer dedicated for stability, but still want to try hosted for speed of iteration.
[10:42] Sofia: That's common. Hosted -> Dedicated is a supported migration path; the Console keeps the same API and rollout configs so it's mostly infra changes behind the scenes.
[10:53] Alex: Okay, final check — anything we missed?
[10:57] Jordan: We just want the parity spreadsheet, security pack, and the bench harness. Also a proposed pilot kickoff slot next Monday morning.
[11:06] Alex: We'll send those today. I'll propose Monday 10am PT for kickoff. Any questions about costs?
[11:12] Marcus: Send a cost estimate for mirrored traffic for the week — rough order of magnitude is fine.
[11:17] Sofia: We'll provide a cost model: token compute estimate, bench run cost, and dedicated monthly snapshots.
[11:25] Jordan: Great, thanks everyone. Quick recap of next steps would be helpful.

[11:30] Alex: Recap: share parity workbook, security pack, bench harness; propose kickoff time; Redwood SE to help wire the mirrored run; customer to sign pilot scope. We'll follow up with links and the action items.
[11:45] [meeting ends, informal goodbyes] Jordan: Thanks! Bye. Alex: Thanks all, bye.
